claims.text: High mixing entropy in noble-metal HEA nanoparticles promotes uniform dispersion of active sites.
High mixing entropy protects noble-metal HEA nanoparticles against sintering.
Noble-metal HEA nanoparticles have better catalytic performance than conventional binary or ternary alloys.
Rapid chemical or thermal reduction can produce a single-phase nanoparticle HEA containing five to seven noble-metal components with homogeneous elemental distribution.
Uniform elemental dispersion produces synergistic electronic effects.
Uniform elemental dispersion maintains a high density of catalytically active sites.
Uniform elemental dispersion prevents particle aggregation.
High mixing entropy stabilizes a single alloy phase.
Entropy-driven single-phase stabilization limits elemental segregation.
Entropy-driven single-phase stabilization limits nanoparticle sintering.
Electronic interactions among homogeneously distributed noble-metal atoms modify surface adsorption energies.
Modified adsorption energies optimize the binding strength of reaction intermediates.
Optimized intermediate binding accelerates reaction kinetics.
Relative to a binary or ternary noble-metal-alloy baseline, the HEA nanoparticles will have significantly higher catalytic activity, such as higher turnover frequency.
Relative to the baseline, the HEA nanoparticles will have better catalytic selectivity.
Relative to the baseline, the HEA nanoparticles will have greater resistance to agglomeration or sintering.
The hypothesis is limited to comparisons having homogeneous elemental distributions and comparable particle sizes.
The hypothesis is limited to reaction and sintering conditions that do not induce phase segregation.
The hypothesis primarily applies to alloys composed of noble metals.
Failure of the HEA nanoparticles to outperform the binary or ternary baseline in catalytic performance and stability under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires homogeneous elemental distribution for the hypothesis to apply, but the falsification rule treats failure to achieve homogeneous distribution as falsification. Such a result would instead violate the stated applicability condition and could reflect unsuccessful material preparation rather than refute the proposed mechanism.
